newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian central banks square up to speculators.
newsitem.headline: Asian central banks square up to speculators.

text.p: Asian central banks are taking the gloves off in the fight to protect their currencies, as speculators cast around for unwilling victims after recent attacks on the Thai baht.
While Thailand did eventually allow the baht to float, and subsequently fall, many speculators got badly burned by defensive measures taken by the Thai authorities during the battle.
Since then, speculators have mainly targeted the Malaysian ringgit, the Philippine peso and the Taiwan dollar.

After aggressive direct foreign exchange intervention late on Tuesday, the Malaysian central bank -- Bank Negara -- on Wednesday launched a verbal offensive, saying it would not hesitate to introduce measures to curb "such speculative activities."
Bank Negara Governor Ahmad Mohamed Don also said interest rates would be allowed to rise.
"Otherwise, we will only be inviting speculative activity in the ringgit if the rates are not allowed to rise given the shortage of ringgit in the market," he said.
Analysts said the remarks were pre-emptive.
"They are being pro-active rather than being reactive," said Andrew Dermot Fung, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered.
"It's always harder to stop something when the market is moving against you, and if they hit the market now it will have a bigger impact than if they try and stop the flow," he added.

The peso has also come under pressure this week, prompting intervention and a sharp rise in interest rates. On Wednesday, President Fidel Ramos talked about "a deliberate effort to undermine the peso" and also spoke of a "media disinformation campaign."

He was referring to newspaper articles this week that quoted Philippine finance secretary Roberto de Ocampo as saying the peso could "devalue" against the U.S. dollar. De Ocampo said he was misquoted.
The Philippine Monetary Board has said it "will intervene strongly using all its available policy weapons to maintain an orderly foreign exchange market and to penalise speculators."
The Taiwan dollar has also come under the gun, closing on Wednesday at an eight-year low against the U.S. dollar. This also prompted central bank intervention.
"There is a lot of concern out there in the region and the currencies as a whole tend to be a lot more nervous, which is probably amplifying the problem," Standard's Fung said.

So who will win? In the case of the baht, many speculators lost money due to the measures Thailand put in place. So to call it a victory for speculators would be over-stating the case, even though eventually the baht was floated.
In the case of the ringgit, analysts do not see a speculative attack succeeding.
An easier target would be the peso, but even here the lack of a forward market and tight liquidity in spot trading means it is protected.
The same goes for the Taiwan dollar, where foreign exchange transactions remain subject to strict reporting requirements and central bank limits, both of which mop up liquidity.

"I find it hard to believe that speculators will actually win against Bank Negara...capital controls are nothing new to Bank Negara, they have done it before and I think if it comes to the crunch, they will do it again," said Chiang Yao Chye, an economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
